calculators.note: PE likely: CTPA immediately if possible. PE unlikely: a D-dimer, with the result within 4 hours if possible.

calculators.title: PERC rule (criteria not met)
calculators.note: Each criterion not met counts 1, so PERC negative is a total of 0. It applies only when clinical suspicion is already low on the overall impression and another diagnosis is feasible (NICE 1.1.16); it has not been validated in COVID-19.

calculators.title: Simplified PESI (sPESI)

items.label: Chronic heart failure or lung disease

bands.text: 0: 30-day mortality 1.0%; low risk only if RV and troponin are normal

calculators.note: Chronic heart failure and chronic lung disease share one point. RV dysfunction on imaging or a raised troponin despite an sPESI of 0 puts the patient in the intermediate-low-risk group (ESC 2019).

calculators.title: CURB-65

items.label: Diastolic 60 or less, or systolic under 90

calculators.note: ATS/IDSA 2019 prefers the PSI to CURB-65 for deciding on admission, always with clinical judgment, and neither score was designed to choose the level of care once a patient is admitted. NICE gives urea in mmol/L.

nodes.chainStep: Airway check; oxygen to 94 to 98% (88 to 92% if at risk of hypercapnic failure); monitoring, ECG and a focused exam
nodes.why: Oxygen is prescribed to a target range: 94 to 98% for most acutely ill patients, 88 to 92% for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, and it is never delayed in a seriously ill patient for a gas. Shortness of breath counts as an anginal equivalent, so the ECG comes early. PE is approached by clinical probability first, not by a D-dimer for everyone.

nodes.why: Intramuscular epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh is first line: 0.01 mg/kg to a maximum of 0.5 mg, repeated every 5 to 15 minutes if symptoms persist. An IV bolus can cause fatal arrhythmias and is not used to start. Antihistamines and glucocorticoids are second line: antihistamines mainly ease the skin, and glucocorticoids may be of no benefit acutely.

Stop epinephrine; IV antihistamine and IV steroid instead, then reassess

nodes.summary: Anaphylaxis that settled: IM epinephrine, observation for a biphasic reaction, auto-injectors and a written action plan; find the trigger.
Refractory anaphylaxis: repeated IM epinephrine, then a monitored IV epinephrine infusion, 20 mL/kg fluid boluses and glucagon on a beta blocker; close observation.
Tension pneumothorax: decompress on the clinical signs without waiting for imaging, then a chest drain; surgical advice to prevent recurrence. The decompression site is not in the open sources read.

nodes.ask: Breathless and in shock; no tension, anaphylaxis or ST elevation. Next?
options: Bedside echo now
D-dimer first; image only if it is raised

nodes.chainStep: Bedside echo now (CTPA instead only if PE is suspected and it is immediately available); oxygen; cautious fluids and a heparin bolus if PE is suspected
nodes.why: With haemodynamic instability, bedside echo or emergency CTPA, whichever the circumstances allow, makes the diagnosis; a D-dimer cannot exclude PE when suspicion is high. When the patient is too unstable for anything but bedside tests, RV dysfunction on echo confirms high-risk PE. Aggressive volume loading can worsen RV function, so fluids are cautious.

nodes.ask: Shock with a dilated right ventricle: high-risk PE. Treatment?
options: Systemic thrombolysis, with unfractionated heparin
Anticoagulation alone, and observe

nodes.why: Primary reperfusion, in most cases systemic thrombolysis, is the treatment of choice for high-risk PE, on a continuous heparin infusion; anticoagulation alone is not enough. Vasopressors support the circulation while reperfusion is given, not instead of it. Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment is for patients in whom thrombolysis is contraindicated or has failed.

orders.dose: 100 mg over 2 hours

nodes.chainStep: Chest x-ray to confirm pneumonia
nodes.why: Clinical signs alone are inaccurate for pneumonia, so the guideline defines it radiographically. Once it is clinically suspected and radiographically confirmed, antibiotics start whatever the procalcitonin. Routine sputum culture is not done in outpatients.
nodes.note: ATS issued a 2025 update on four questions (lung ultrasound for diagnosis, antibiotics when a virus test is positive, antibiotic duration, corticosteroids); its full text was not reachable for this version.

outcomes.if: Pneumonia; a new infiltrate
No infiltrate

nodes.ask: Pneumonia on the film. Where to treat?
options: Clinical judgment plus the PSI or CURB-65
CURB-65 alone, without clinical judgment
The procalcitonin level decides the site
The white count decides the site of care
nodes.chainStep: Clinical judgment plus PSI (preferred) or CURB-65 for admission; ICU for vasopressors or ventilation; minor criteria and judgment guide the rest
nodes.why: A validated prognostic rule, the PSI in preference to CURB-65, is used together with clinical judgment to decide on admission. Hypotension needing vasopressors or respiratory failure needing ventilation goes straight to the ICU; otherwise the 2007 minor criteria with judgment guide higher-intensity care. Severe CAP is one major or 3 or more minor criteria. Some patients need admission for other reasons, such as being unable to keep up oral intake.

orders.item: Minor criteria (3 or more is severe)
orders.dose: Respiratory rate 30 or more, PaO2/FiO2 250 or less, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, BUN 20 mg/dL or more, white count under 4,000, platelets under 100,000, temperature under 36, hypotension needing aggressive fluids
Septic shock needing vasopressors; respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation

outcomes.if: Outpatient; low risk on PSI and judgment
Ward; admitted, not severe
Severe; 1 major or 3 or more minor criteria

nodes.ask: Outpatient CAP, no comorbidity, no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk. Antibiotic?
options: Amoxicillin or doxycycline if healthy; broader cover if comorbid
Azithromycin alone, whatever the local macrolide resistance
A respiratory fluoroquinolone first-line if healthy
Amoxicillin-clavulanate plus azithromycin, as for comorbid patients
nodes.chainStep: Healthy: amoxicillin 1 g three times daily or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; with comorbidity: amoxicillin-clavulanate or a cephalosporin plus a macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone
nodes.why: A healthy adult gets amoxicillin or doxycycline; a macrolide alone only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is under 25%. Chronic heart, lung, liver or renal disease, diabetes, alcoholism, malignancy or asplenia call for amoxicillin-clavulanate or a cephalosporin with a macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone.

orders.dose: Amoxicillin 1 g three times daily, or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, or a macrolide (azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg daily, or clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily) only where pneumococcal macrolide resistance is under 25%

Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily (or 500/125 mg three times daily, or 2,000/125 mg twice daily), or cefpodoxime 200 mg or cefuroxime 500 mg twice daily, plus azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline 100 mg twice daily; or levofloxacin 750 mg, moxifloxacin 400 mg or gemifloxacin 320 mg daily alone
Guided by clinical stability; until stable and no less than a total of 5 days
orders.note: The 2025 ATS update on duration was not read.

nodes.ask: Admitted to the ward, not severe, no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk. Regimen?
options: Beta-lactam plus macrolide, or a fluoroquinolone alone
Ceftriaxone alone, since atypical cover adds nothing
Vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam
Azithromycin alone, oral, for the whole course
nodes.chainStep: Ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g daily plus azithromycin 500 mg daily, or levofloxacin 750 mg daily alone
nodes.why: Nonsevere inpatients without MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors get a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone; a beta-lactam with doxycycline is the third option when both are contraindicated. MRSA or Pseudomonas cover is added only for locally validated risk factors.

orders.dose: Ampicillin-sulbactam 1.5 to 3 g every 6 h, cefotaxime 1 to 2 g every 8 h, ceftriaxone 1 to 2 g daily, or ceftaroline 600 mg every 12 h
Azithromycin 500 mg daily or clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily
Levofloxacin 750 mg daily or moxifloxacin 400 mg daily
Beta-lactam plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
Not routinely in nonsevere CAP

nodes.ask: Severe CAP by the minor criteria, no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk. Regimen?
options: Beta-lactam plus either a macrolide or a fluoroquinolone
A respiratory fluoroquinolone alone, given IV
Ceftriaxone alone, at the higher daily dose
Vancomycin plus cefepime, as for hospital-acquired
nodes.chainStep: Beta-lactam plus macrolide (or beta-lactam plus respiratory fluoroquinolone); blood and sputum cultures before treatment; pneumococcal and Legionella urine antigens
nodes.why: Severe CAP without MRSA or Pseudomonas risk gets a beta-lactam with a macrolide, or a beta-lactam with a respiratory fluoroquinolone; doses are as for the ward. Severe disease is the setting for pretreatment blood and sputum cultures and for pneumococcal and Legionella urine antigens.

orders.dose: Pretreatment blood cultures and sputum Gram stain and culture
Pneumococcal and Legionella; Legionella culture or NAAT of lower respiratory secretions
Only with locally validated risk factors: vancomycin 15 mg/kg every 12 h or linezolid 600 mg every 12 h; piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 h or cefepime 2 g every 8 h, among others
ATS/IDSA 2019 suggested not routinely using them in severe CAP; the 2025 ATS update and the 2024 SCCM update both address this and were not read

nodes.summary: Outpatient CAP: amoxicillin or doxycycline when healthy; with comorbidity, amoxicillin-clavulanate or a cephalosporin plus a macrolide or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone.

Inpatient CAP: a beta-lactam plus a macrolide, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone on the ward; when severe, a beta-lactam with a macrolide or a fluoroquinolone, cultures and urine antigens; MRSA or Pseudomonas cover only for those at risk.
No infiltrate: outside the guideline, which covers radiographically confirmed CAP; not covered further here.

nodes.ask: Sudden one-sided pleuritic chest pain, stable. Next?
options: Chest x-ray
Needle aspiration now, before imaging
CT chest before any x-ray
A D-dimer before any imaging
nodes.chainStep: Chest x-ray; CT if it is uncertain
nodes.why: Outside tension pneumothorax, a recent image confirms the pneumothorax and its side before any procedure. The x-ray also shows whether there is enough of a rim to intervene safely, usually 2 cm or more on the film, or any size on CT that can be safely reached. Breathlessness with pleuritic pain also earns a chest x-ray when PE is in the frame.

sources.where: Preprocedural imaging in the operative position and marking of position

outcomes.if: Primary, minimal symptoms; no lung disease, little pain or breathlessness
Primary, symptomatic; no high-risk features
High risk or secondary; lung disease, 50 or older and smoking, hypoxia
No pneumothorax

nodes.ask: Primary pneumothorax, minimal symptoms. Management?
options: Conservative care, outpatient review and a follow-up x-ray
Chest drain and admission until the lung is up
Thoracic surgery now, to prevent a recurrence
Needle aspiration now, since the rim is visible
nodes.chainStep: Conservative care: outpatient review, follow-up chest x-ray at 2 to 4 weeks, no commercial flights until resolved, stop smoking
nodes.why: Conservative management can be considered for minimally symptomatic or asymptomatic primary pneumothorax regardless of size, and it shortens the hospital stay compared with a drain. Patients managed by observation return for an x-ray at 2 to 4 weeks and do not fly until the pneumothorax has resolved.

sources.where: A1 recommendations and evidence statements; discharge advice, flying and activity

orders.dose: At 2 to 4 weeks after observation or needle aspiration
Not until radiological resolution; then 7 days after the x-ray shows it
Advise cessation: it raises the risk of recurrence

nodes.ask: Primary pneumothorax, breathless, rim over 2 cm, no high-risk features. Management?
options: Ambulatory device, needle aspiration or a drain, by patient choice
Thoracic surgery now, at this first episode
Chemical pleurodesis through a chest drain
Chest drain mandatory, because the rim is over 2 cm
nodes.chainStep: Ambulatory device, needle aspiration or chest drain, chosen with the patient; review, and a follow-up x-ray at 2 to 4 weeks
nodes.why: Size no longer decides on intervention, only whether it is safe, usually at 2 cm or more. An ambulatory device where the service exists, needle aspiration or a drain are the options, chosen with the patient's priority; needle aspiration shortens the stay but more often needs a further procedure. Surgery at a first episode is considered when preventing recurrence matters most, such as after tension or in high-risk occupations; chemical pleurodesis is considered to prevent recurrent secondary pneumothorax.

sources.where: Definitions and treatment principles; A1 recommendations, evidence statements and good practice point; Appendix 1

orders.dose: At 2 to 4 weeks after needle aspiration
Not until radiological resolution; then 7 days after the x-ray shows it

nodes.ask: Pneumothorax with lung disease, or 50 or older and smoking; breathless. Management?
options: Chest drain and inpatient review
Conservative care at home
Needle aspiration and discharge
Thoracic surgery before any drain
nodes.chainStep: Chest drain with inpatient review; surgical advice when a first secondary pneumothorax caused significant physiological compromise
nodes.why: Chest drains are centred on patients with high-risk characteristics: underlying lung disease, age 50 or more with a significant smoking history, significant hypoxia, bilateral pneumothorax, haemopneumothorax or haemodynamic compromise. A first secondary pneumothorax with significant physiological compromise earns surgical advice, and pleurodesis can be considered where a recurrence would be hazardous.

sources.where: Definitions and treatment principles; Appendix 1; A1 recommendations; accepted indications for surgical advice

orders.dose: Talc pleurodesis can be considered at the first episode when a recurrence would be hazardous (for example severe COPD)

nodes.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax: managed by symptoms, not size: conservative care when minimally symptomatic, otherwise an ambulatory device, needle aspiration or a drain; x-ray follow-up at 2 to 4 weeks.
High-risk or secondary pneumothorax: chest drain and inpatient review; surgical advice or pleurodesis to prevent recurrence.

nodes.ask: PE is possible and the patient is stable. Next?
options: Two-level Wells score for the clinical probability
A D-dimer, whatever the clinical probability
V/Q scan first, before any scoring
CTPA first, then estimate the clinical probability
nodes.chainStep: Two-level Wells score (consider PERC first when suspicion is low); chest x-ray to exclude other causes
nodes.why: In stable patients the strategy rests on clinical probability, from judgment or a validated rule; NICE uses the two-level Wells score, over 4 points PE likely. When suspicion is low and another diagnosis is feasible, the PERC rule can show that no test is needed. A D-dimer is not used when probability is high, because a normal result does not exclude PE.

orders.dose: DVT signs 3; an alternative diagnosis less likely than PE 3; heart rate over 100: 1.5; immobilization over 3 days or surgery in 4 weeks 1.5; previous DVT or PE 1.5; haemoptysis 1; malignancy 1. Over 4 points: PE likely
Consider when suspicion is low on the overall impression and other diagnoses are feasible
To exclude other causes

nodes.note: The 2026 AHA/ACC acute PE guideline introduces its own clinical categories; its full text was not reachable, so this branch follows ESC 2019, NICE NG158 and ASH 2020.

outcomes.if: PE unlikely; 4 points or less
PE likely; more than 4 points
PERC negative; low suspicion, all 8 criteria met

orders.dose: Age under 50; pulse under 100; SaO2 over 94%; no unilateral leg swelling; no haemoptysis; no recent trauma or surgery; no history of VTE; no oral hormone use

outcomes.if: PERC not satisfied

nodes.ask: PE unlikely on Wells; PERC not satisfied. Next?
options: D-dimer; CTPA only if it is positive
CTPA now, without a D-dimer
Discharge home without any test
A V/Q scan now, instead of a D-dimer
nodes.chainStep: D-dimer (age-adjusted over 50), result within 4 hours or interim anticoagulation while waiting; CTPA if positive
nodes.why: With PE unlikely, a D-dimer, preferably highly sensitive, saves imaging: after a negative result the 3-month risk untreated was under 1%, so PE is set aside; a positive one goes to CTPA. If the result will take more than 4 hours, interim anticoagulation covers the wait. Over 50, an age-adjusted cutoff may be used.

orders.dose: Result within 4 hours if possible; otherwise interim therapeutic anticoagulation while waiting
Consider an age-adjusted threshold for people over 50

outcomes.if: Negative; below the cutoff
Positive

nodes.ask: PE likely, or a positive D-dimer. Next?
options: CTPA, or a V/Q scan if contrast is a problem
Repeat the D-dimer in 24 hours and compare
MR angiography to spare the radiation
Thrombolysis first, then the scan
nodes.chainStep: Anticoagulate now when clinical probability is high or intermediate (LMWH or fondaparinux); CTPA immediately (V/Q SPECT or planar V/Q if contrast allergy, creatinine clearance under 30 or high radiation risk)
nodes.why: A likely Wells score, or a positive D-dimer, goes to CTPA immediately if possible; contrast allergy, creatinine clearance under 30 mL/min or a high radiation risk make V/Q the alternative. If imaging cannot be done at once, interim anticoagulation is given. MR angiography is not used to rule out PE.

orders.dose: Without delay when clinical probability is high or intermediate; NICE offers interim anticoagulation if imaging cannot be done immediately; parenterally, LMWH or fondaparinux over UFH for most

outcomes.if: PE; a segmental or more proximal filling defect
Normal

orders.dose: Consider a proximal leg vein ultrasound

nodes.ask: PE on CTPA, blood pressure normal. Next?
options: Grade the risk: sPESI, RV on imaging, troponin
Systemic thrombolysis now, before any grading
An IVC filter to protect against a further clot
Discharge home before any risk grading
nodes.chainStep: sPESI (or PESI), RV size on CT or echo, and troponin to grade the risk
nodes.why: Without haemodynamic instability, PE is stratified further into intermediate and low risk. The right ventricle is assessed on imaging or by biomarkers even when the PESI is low or the sPESI negative, because RV dysfunction can hide behind a reassuring score.

outcomes.if: Low risk; sPESI 0, RV and troponin normal
Intermediate risk; sPESI 1 or more, or RV dysfunction or raised troponin

nodes.ask: Low-risk PE, good support at home. Disposition?
options: Home on apixaban or rivaroxaban, with a follow-up plan
Admit for 5 days of IV heparin, then an oral agent
Low-dose thrombolysis, then home the next day
LMWH bridged to warfarin as first choice
nodes.chainStep: Home treatment on apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least 3 months, with written warning signs and direct contact with a thrombosis team
nodes.why: Low-risk PE is treated at home when outpatient care and anticoagulation can be provided, using a validated risk tool. Apixaban or rivaroxaban is offered first, DOACs over VKAs, for at least 3 months, with written information on warning signs and direct contact details.

orders.dose: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily; or rivaroxaban 15 mg twice daily with food for 21 days, then 20 mg once daily with food
At least 3 months
Written information on warning symptoms; direct contact with a thrombosis team; out-of-hours contacts

nodes.ask: PE, normotensive, sPESI 1 or more or a strained right ventricle. Treatment?
options: Admit and anticoagulate; no routine thrombolysis
Systemic thrombolysis now, then anticoagulate
Anticoagulate, plus an IVC filter for safety
Home treatment today on an oral anticoagulant
nodes.chainStep: Admit; LMWH or fondaparinux (or a DOAC); monitor when RV dysfunction and troponin are both abnormal; rescue thrombolysis if instability develops
nodes.why: Normotensive patients with any marker of raised risk are admitted. Routine primary thrombolysis is not recommended without instability, even with RV dysfunction: the bleeding risk outweighs the benefit. RV dysfunction with a positive troponin earns monitoring over the first hours or days, and rescue thrombolysis or embolectomy is kept for those who deteriorate.

orders.dose: LMWH or fondaparinux over UFH for most
A NOAC in preference to a VKA when eligible
Monitor over the first hours or days; LMWH for the first 2 to 3 days before switching to oral
Not with haemodynamic stability, with or without RV dysfunction
Rescue thrombolysis, or surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment
Not routinely

nodes.summary: PE excluded (a negative D-dimer with PE unlikely, or a normal CTPA): think of other causes and explain when to come back; a leg ultrasound if DVT is still suspected.
No further PE testing; think of other causes.
Low-risk PE: home on apixaban or rivaroxaban for at least 3 months, with written warning signs and direct contact details.
Intermediate-risk PE: admitted and anticoagulated, no routine thrombolysis, monitoring when the right ventricle and troponin are both abnormal, rescue reperfusion if it turns unstable.

cases.label: Tension pneumothorax
cases.vignette: 26-year-old man, sudden left chest pain an hour ago, now gasping and anxious. HR 134, BP 80/48, RR 36, SpO2 82% on air.

results.front: Trachea deviated to the right; left chest hyperresonant with no breath sounds; neck veins distended. ECG: sinus tachycardia.

cases.label: Anaphylaxis that settles
cases.vignette: 29-year-old woman, stung by a wasp 10 minutes ago: hives, swollen lips, a hoarse voice and noisy breathing. Weight 60 kg. BP 102/66, HR 118, SpO2 93%.

results.front: Inspiratory stridor and wheeze, generalized hives, lip swelling. ECG: sinus tachycardia.
results.anaph_response: Five minutes after one IM dose: stridor gone, wheeze easing, BP 118/74, SpO2 97%.

cases.label: Refractory anaphylaxis on a beta blocker
cases.vignette: 58-year-old man on metoprolol, collapsed 15 minutes after a shrimp dinner: flushed, wheezy, faint. Weight 80 kg. BP 72/40, HR 64.

results.front: Generalized hives and wheeze, BP 72/40. ECG: sinus rhythm, no ST change.
results.anaph_response: After two IM doses 5 minutes apart and a 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus: BP 76/44, still wheezy.

cases.label: Breathlessness as an anginal equivalent
cases.vignette: 66-year-old woman with diabetes, an hour of breathlessness and sweating, no chest pain. BP 132/78, HR 96, SpO2 94%.

results.front: ECG: 2 mm ST elevation in V2 to V5. Chest clear, no rash, both sides air entry equal.

cases.label: High-risk PE
cases.vignette: 48-year-old woman on the combined pill, a swollen left calf for a week, collapsed at home breathless. No recent surgery, trauma, stroke or bleeding. BP 78/50, HR 128, SpO2 84%.

results.front: Cold peripheries, raised neck veins, clear chest with equal air entry, no rash or stridor. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST elevation.
results.shock_echo_result: Too unstable to leave resus. Bedside echo: right ventricle larger than the left, poorly contracting; left ventricle small and vigorous; no effusion.

cases.label: Shock without RV dysfunction
cases.vignette: 71-year-old man with a past myocardial infarction, breathless and clammy. BP 82/54, HR 104, SpO2 89%.

results.front: Cold hands, crackles to the mid-zones, no rash or stridor. ECG: old Q waves, no ST elevation or new ischemic change.
results.shock_echo_result: Bedside echo: right ventricle normal size; left ventricle dilated and poorly contracting.

cases.label: Moderate asthma, good response
cases.vignette: 24-year-old woman with asthma, two days of wheeze after a cold, speaking in sentences. RR 22, HR 104, SpO2 95%.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Known asthma; widespread wheeze, no stridor, no rash.
results.asthma_response: After three SABA doses and oral prednisone: PEF 78% of best, holding 60 minutes after the last dose; no distress.

cases.label: Severe asthma, poor response
cases.vignette: 31-year-old man with asthma and two past ICU admissions, breathless at rest, speaking in phrases. RR 30, HR 122, SpO2 92%.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Known asthma; loud wheeze both sides, accessory muscles working, no stridor.
results.asthma_response: After an hour of SABA, ipratropium and prednisone: PEF 35% of predicted, PCO2 40 mm Hg, alert.

cases.label: Severe asthma, incomplete response
cases.vignette: 45-year-old woman with asthma, breathless at rest since the morning. RR 28, HR 112, SpO2 93%.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Known asthma; widespread wheeze, no stridor.
results.asthma_response: After treatment: PEF 55% of predicted, still mildly breathless.

cases.label: Life-threatening asthma
cases.vignette: 19-year-old with asthma brought in by friends, too breathless to speak, drowsy. RR 8, HR 132, SpO2 86% on oxygen.

results.front: BP 118/70. No rash or stridor; ECG: sinus tachycardia, no ST change.
results.findings: Known asthma; a quiet chest with barely any air movement.
results.asthma_sev: Drowsy and confused; cannot attempt a peak flow.

cases.label: COPD exacerbation needing NIV
cases.vignette: 69-year-old man with COPD, three days of more breathlessness and green sputum. RR 28, HR 104, SpO2 86% on air, alert.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Known COPD; wheeze and prolonged expiration; sputum green and more than usual; no leg swelling.
results.copd_cxr: Chest x-ray: hyperinflated lungs, no consolidation.
results.copd_gas: After an hour of nebulizers, prednisolone and an antibiotic, on a 28% Venturi: pH 7.29, PaCO2 67 mm Hg (8.9 kPa).

cases.label: COPD exacerbation without acidosis
cases.vignette: 74-year-old woman with COPD, more breathless for two days with yellow sputum. RR 24, HR 96, SpO2 89% on air.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Known COPD; scattered wheeze; sputum yellow and thicker than usual.
results.copd_cxr: Chest x-ray: hyperinflated lungs, no consolidation.
results.copd_gas: On a 24% Venturi after treatment: pH 7.38, PaCO2 45 mm Hg (6.0 kPa).

cases.label: Hypertensive pulmonary edema
cases.vignette: 72-year-old woman with no known heart failure, woke gasping, cannot lie flat. BP 214/118, HR 112, RR 34, SpO2 84% on air, alert.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG: sinus tachycardia, left ventricular hypertrophy, no ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Crackles to the apices, raised neck veins, mild ankle edema.
results.ahf_resp: Arterial gas: pH 7.24; she is working hard to breathe, still alert.

cases.label: Acute heart failure, normal pressure
cases.vignette: 79-year-old man with no known heart failure, a week of worsening breathlessness, two pillows at night, ankles swelling, 4 kg heavier. BP 132/80, HR 92, SpO2 91%.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Bibasal crackles, neck veins raised, pitting edema to the knees.
results.ahf_resp: Arterial gas: pH 7.41; breathing comfortably at rest.

cases.label: Heart failure ruled out, PE unlikely
cases.vignette: 68-year-old woman, two weeks of breathlessness on exertion and swollen ankles. No known heart failure. BP 138/84, HR 88, SpO2 95%.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Both ankles puffy, a few basal crackles, neck veins not raised.
results.ahf_resp: Arterial gas: pH 7.40; comfortable at rest.
results.pe_score: Wells 3: no other diagnosis is more likely than PE; no DVT signs, heart rate under 100, no immobility, surgery, previous VTE, haemoptysis or cancer.

cases.label: Pneumonia treated at home
cases.vignette: 34-year-old man, no medical history, three days of fever and a productive cough. RR 20, HR 96, BP 124/76, SpO2 96%, temperature 38.6.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Bronchial breathing and crackles at the right base.
results.cap_result: Chest x-ray: right lower lobe consolidation.
results.cap_site: PSI class I; eating and drinking, good support at home; no recent hospital stay or IV antibiotics.

cases.label: Pneumonia on the ward
cases.vignette: 67-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, fever, cough and breathlessness. RR 24, HR 102, BP 128/74, SpO2 92%, temperature 38.9.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Crackles at the left base.
results.cap_result: Chest x-ray: left lower lobe consolidation.
results.cap_site: Vomiting and unable to keep up oral intake, so admitted; alert, RR 24, BUN 16 mg/dL (urea 5.7 mmol/L), no minor criteria met; no MRSA or Pseudomonas in the past, no hospital stay or IV antibiotics in 90 days.

cases.label: Severe pneumonia by minor criteria
cases.vignette: 58-year-old man, two days of fever and cough, now muddled. RR 32, HR 116, BP 104/62, SpO2 84% on air, temperature 39.4.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Crackles and bronchial breathing over both lower zones.
results.cap_result: Chest x-ray: consolidation in both lower lobes.
results.cap_site: Confused, RR 32, BUN 28 mg/dL (urea 10.0 mmol/L), PaO2/FiO2 230, multilobar: 5 minor criteria; no vasopressor or ventilator needed; no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk.

cases.label: Fever and cough, clear film
cases.vignette: 41-year-old woman, two days of fever and a dry cough. RR 18, HR 92, BP 122/78, SpO2 97%, temperature 38.2.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: A few crackles at the right base.
results.cap_result: Chest x-ray: clear lungs, no infiltrate.

cases.label: Small primary pneumothorax, few symptoms
cases.vignette: 22-year-old tall man, sudden sharp left chest pain at rest 6 hours ago, now mild, not breathless. HR 82, BP 122/74, SpO2 98%.

cases.label: Symptomatic primary pneumothorax

cases.label: Secondary pneumothorax in COPD
cases.vignette: 67-year-old man with COPD who smokes, sudden worse breathlessness and right chest pain, no change in sputum. HR 108, BP 136/80, SpO2 90% on air.

cases.label: No pneumothorax, then PE ruled out

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Breath sounds perhaps a little quieter on the right; no wheeze, crackles or leg swelling.
results.ptx_result: Chest x-ray: no pneumothorax, lungs clear.
results.pe_score: Wells 3: no other diagnosis is more likely than PE; heart rate under 100, no DVT signs, immobility, surgery, previous VTE, haemoptysis or cancer.
results.pe_perc: PERC not satisfied: she is 52 and takes estrogen.

cases.label: Low-risk PE, home
cases.vignette: 36-year-old woman, two days of breathlessness after a long flight, a painful swollen right calf. HR 92, BP 126/80, SpO2 95%. Lives with her partner.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
results.findings: Chest clear; right calf swollen and tender along the deep veins.
results.pe_score: Wells 6: DVT signs 3, no other diagnosis more likely than PE 3.
results.ctpa_result: CTPA: segmental filling defects in the right lower lobe.
results.pe_risk_result: sPESI 0; RV/LV ratio normal on CT; troponin normal.

cases.label: Intermediate-risk PE
cases.vignette: 63-year-old man, 10 days after a knee replacement, sudden breathlessness this morning. HR 112, BP 124/78, SpO2 91%.

results.front: No tension, anaphylaxis or shock; ECG without ST elevation or new ischemia.
